summary.title: Part 02 — 50 BC, 1952 & 5 April 1991: Lucretius's Shaped Atoms, John Amoore's Stereochemical Locks & Linda Buck and Richard Axel's 1,000-Gene Shock

plates.quality_reason: Quality: readable faces (British biochemist John Amoore at Oxford in 1952 fitting shaped molecular models into stereochemical receptor sockets, dissolving to Linda Buck and Richard Axel at Columbia University on 5 April 1991 discovering the ~1,000-gene mammalian / ~400-gene human 7-transmembrane GPCR olfactory receptor family).
plates.prompt: Premium Animistry-class 3D cartoon. Split period scene: on the left in 1952 Oxford, biochemist John Amoore fits wooden ball-and-stick odour models into carved sockets; on the right in April 1991 New York, Linda Buck and Richard Axel celebrate beside a gel revealing hundreds of seven-transmembrane smell receptor genes. No readable words or numbers anywhere. Silent. Continuous motion through the final frame. No Explorer. No Orbit.

plates.quality_reason: Flow-first: a teach diagram, chart, counter or timeline is a £0 code graphic. No Flow mint.
plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked mammalian & human olfactory receptor multigene family chart from Buck & Axel (5 April 1991, Cell 65: 175–187) shows 7-transmembrane GPCR odorant receptors comprising ~1,000 genes in rodents and ~390–400 functional genes (+ ~460 pseudogenes) in humans, representing ~3–4% of the entire mammalian proteome.

teach_overlay.label: 5 APR 1991 BUCK & AXEL: ~1,000 MAMMALIAN / ~400 HUMAN 7-TM GPCR SMELL GENES (~3% OF ALL HUMAN GENES)
teach_overlay.detail: Inked mammalian & human olfactory receptor multigene family chart on period paper from Buck & Axel (5 April 1991, Cell 65: 175–187) showing 7-transmembrane GPCR odorant receptors comprising ~1,000 genes in rodents and ~390–400 functional genes (+ ~460 pseudogenes) in humans, representing ~3–4% of the entire mammalian proteome
teach_overlay.scale: out of the roughly twenty thousand protein-coding genes that build your entire body — your heart, brain, bones, and muscles — roughly one out of every thirty genes is dedicated solely to helping you smell
